newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sugar crop plan holds few surprises - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sugar crop plan holds few surprises - analyst.

text.p: Brazil's 1997/98 sugar crop plan contains few surprises in terms of overall figures but has inconsistencies in its internal allocations, said an independent consultant.

"The plan is full of inconsistencies on an internal level. There are distortions in allocations on regional and state levels and between individual factories," said Aloisio Sotero of DataNet-Agricommodities.

For one thing, the plan which forecast total production of 13.48 million tonnes sugar this coming crop year, foresees internal consumption at 8.10 million tonnes against 8.48 million tonnes in the 1996/97 crop plan.
"At the very least, it should be the same as last year but it really should have grown if only because of population growth," Sotero said.
The plan also sets out production goals of anhydrous and hydrous alcohol which exceed demand, he added.
In the north/northeast, the government's own figures are for demand of one million cubic meters of anhydrous and 1.35 million in hydrous alcohol, Sotero said.
Production of combustibles however should be 2.7 million cubic meters according to the plan.

In the key center-south region, production of 5.07 million cubic meters anhydrous and 7.95 million hydrous alcohol both exceed consumption estimates of 4.60 million and 7.5 million cubic meters respectively.
Moreover the crop plan has made provision for the possible import of 700,000 cubic meters of methanol into the center-south region, should there be insufficient supply of hydrous alcohol.
The government has said from the outset of talks on the 1997/98 crop plan that its priority was to produce enough alcohol to be able to eliminate the need for imports.

Hence, despite expectations of a higher cane crop, the plan envisages slightly less sugar production (13.68 million tonnes in 1996/97) and significantly higher total alcohol production of 16.73 million cubic meters against 13.89 million last year.
Sotero said he felt the government however was being ambitious in its production ideas and the crop plan was more what it would like to see produced rather than actual estimates.
An export allocation of 5.39 million tonnes, up marginally from 5.2 million last year, was also an initial figure, he said.
Working on the basis of a sugar cane crop of around 315 million tonnes, Brazil had the sugar export potential of between six and 6.5 million tonnes, he said.
Currently the government controls the flow of exports with an export tax, last year of up to 40 percent, which applies to sugars in excess of the original export quota.
The sugar industry in the center-south has been lobbying for exports to be liberated and even now expectations are that the government could open up exports even this year.

"We understand that in the next two months the National Monetary Council could meet and decide to reduce to zero the tax on exports over and above those allowed in the crop plan, in effect liberating exports," one private sector official said.

"We are not pushing for this to increase exports. This has nothing to do with the actual amount exported, we just want individual factories to be able to export more than their quota, if they can, without having to buy quota from people who have and never had sugar to ship," he added.
A working group of government officials is to meet over the next two months to look at possible new mechanisms to liberate additional exports from tariffs, Sotero said.
((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
